Issued at 152 AM CDT Tue Sep 1 2026

Though Tonight...

Early morning GOES-19 water vapor imagery depicts an expansive 
summer-like heat dome centered over the middle Mississippi River
Valley with RAP-analyzed 500mb heights near 5960m over Paducah,
Kentucky. Meanwhile, an upper-level low was centered near the 
Manitoba and Ontario borders in southern Canada. Quasi-zonal 
flow stretches between the upper-level low to the north and heat
dome to the south from the Black Hills region eastward through 
the Lower Great Lakes. Closer to the surface, an expansive 
region of unseasonably moist low-level air characterized by dew 
points in the low to mid 70s encompasses much of the Great 
Lakes, Upper Mississippi River, and middle Mississippi River 
valleys. The large-scale pattern is more typical of the middle 
of July than the first day of September. 

The primary concern today are dangerous heat. Owing to the very
wet summer (90 day observed precipitation departures were 200 
to 300% of normal across parts of Illinois and Indiana), 
agricultural evapotranspiration is still in full swing. Dew 
points yesterday climbed into the mid to upper 70s across much 
of the forecast area, and frankly there are no reasons why the 
same won't happen today. With 850mb temperatures peaking in the 
+22 to +23 range today and tomorrow, dry bulb high temperatures 
should have no problem reaching the low to mid 90s. When 
combined with dew points in the mid to upper 70s, widespread 
heat index values of 105 to locally 110F (wet bulb globe 
temperatures of 87 to 90F) appear to be a good bet today. 

The only fly in the ointment is the low probability threat for 
thunderstorms and associated free air conditioning (whether by 
cloud cover or precipitation). Early this morning, have been 
keeping a close eye on an elongated west-to-east band of ACCAS 
extending from near Omaha, Nebraska to Davenport, Iowa. Per the 
00Z RAOBs from OAX and DVN, the ACCAS field is rooted at the 
base of an EML plume in which lapse rates range from 7.5 to 8 
K/km from 850 to 500 mb. Over the past hour or two, the ACCAS 
field has gotten increasingly agitated east of Omaha, presumably
owing to increasing low-level confluence on the nose of a 
modest but nevertheless intensifying 850mb low-level jet and at 
least a glancing blow of upper-level diffluence in the right 
entrance region of a jet streak propagating into the Great 
Lakes.

In the absence of more pronounced forcing for ascent, it seems 
like the most likely scenario is for thunderstorms to struggle 
to develop and maintain themselves across Iowa early this 
morning. However, should they develop and become established, 
they will have access to a highway of moisture-laden instability
(MUCAPE >3000 J/kg) that points directly to Chicago. When also 
considering access to 30 to 35kt of westerly upper-level flow on
the southern edge of the aforementioned jet streak, any 
established storm would be prone to developing into an eastward-
racing cluster with a threat for damaging winds (again, 
sweeping across much of our area). Timing would be from mid-
morning to early afternoon (call it 9 AM to 3 PM from west to
east). At this point, the chance of this outcome seems low 
(call it a 10 to 20% probability), but will continue to watch 
trends across Iowa this morning in case the odds start to turn. 

Will also note there is a threat for thunderstorms to develop 
at any point this afternoon when instability is maximized, 
though am currently not seeing really any mechanisms to force 
ascent beyond the window from this morning within the neutral 
mid-level height-tendency regime. 

With the more likely scenario appearing to be being no storms 
today, will go ahead and expand the Heat Advisory to now 
encompass the entire area. While the Heat Advisory will expire 
at 9 PM, tonight will still be balmy with overnight lows in the 
low to mid 70s. 


Wednesday...

On Wednesday, ensemble guidance is in fair agreement that an 
upper-level shortwave embedded in the upper-level anticyclonic 
flow around the ridge will propagate into the Upper Mississippi 
River Valley and upper Great Lakes. Depending on the evolution 
of thunderstorms tonight in the northern Plains, can easily 
envision an MCS or two riding across Minnesota, central 
Wisconsin, and Lower Michigan on Wednesday. With all forcing 
remaining well north of our area, the chance for storms on 
Wednesday will be even lower than today. 

Interestingly, guidance suggests dew points may be a touch 
lower on Wednesday compared to today which would lead to heat 
index values more in the range of 100 to 105 versus 105 to
110F. However, will continue to lean on evapotranspiration 
being a big facor and forecast another day with dangerous heat.
